authoredSolutions.26: Bohr pictured the electron travelling in a well-defined circular orbit of fixed radius. The quantum mechanical model rejects this: the Heisenberg uncertainty principle forbids simultaneously fixing the position and momentum of an electron, so a definite circular path cannot be assigned. The electron is instead described by an orbital, a region of probability given by the square of the wave function. The other three postulates survive in the quantum mechanical description: stationary states of constant energy exist (B), an atom in a stationary state does not radiate (A), and a photon of energy \(\Delta E = h\nu\) is emitted when the electron drops to a lower stationary state (C). Hence (D).
authoredSolutions.27: Statement I has two clauses and only one of them is right. Bond enthalpies: \(N-N \approx 159\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\) against \(P-P \approx 213\) kJ mol\(^{-1}\), so the N-N single bond really is weaker (lone-pair repulsion on the small nitrogen atoms). But bond lengths are \(N-N \approx 145\) pm and \(P-P \approx 221\) pm, so N-N is much SHORTER, not longer. Statement I is therefore false. Statement II is also false: on descending group 15 the inert pair effect makes the +3 state progressively MORE stable, so Sb(III) and Bi(III) are perfectly stable and do not disproportionate. Only nitrogen(III), as \(HNO_{2}\), disproportionates, and that is a special case rather than a group property. Both statements false, so (B).
authoredSolutions.28: Statement I is true. \(K_{c}\) is fixed by \(\Delta G^{\circ} = -RT \ln K\), a difference of standard state properties of reactants and products alone. A catalyst supplies an alternative lower-energy path and speeds both forward and reverse reactions by the same factor, so it changes only how fast equilibrium is reached, never \(K_{c}\) at fixed temperature. Statement II is true in the sense intended: a homogeneous catalyst is in the SAME phase as the reaction mixture, so it is itself a component of that mixture. Its presence dilutes the system and it can tie up reactant as catalyst-substrate intermediates, so the actual amounts of reactants and products present at equilibrium can differ from those in the uncatalysed mixture even though the ratio fixed by \(K_{c}\) is unchanged. A heterogeneous catalyst, being in a separate phase, cannot do this. Both statements true, so (B).
authoredSolutions.29: Spin-only moment \(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\) B.M. Setting \(\sqrt{n(n+2)} = 4.9\) gives \(n(n+2) = 24\), so \(n = 4\) unpaired electrons. Now count d electrons: \(Cr^{2+}\) is \(d^{4}\) (4 unpaired) yes; \(Fe^{2+}\) is \(d^{6}\), high spin \(t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}\) (4 unpaired) yes; \(Fe^{3+}\) is \(d^{5}\) (5 unpaired, 5.92 B.M.) no; \(Co^{2+}\) is \(d^{7}\) (3 unpaired, 3.87 B.M.) no; \(Mn^{3+}\) is \(d^{4}\) (4 unpaired) yes. So A, B and E, which is option (D).
authoredSolutions.31: Fructose is a 2-ketohexose, so the Fischer projection runs \(CH_{2}OH\) (C1), \(C=O\) (C2), then three stereocentres C3, C4, C5, then \(CH_{2}OH\) (C6). D-fructose has OH on the LEFT at C3 and on the RIGHT at C4 and C5. L-fructose is the complete mirror image, so it must have OH on the RIGHT at C3 and on the LEFT at C4 and C5, the reference C5 hydroxyl on the left being what makes it L. Only the third structure shows OH right at C3 and OH left at C4 and C5; the first has right-right-left, the second left-left-left and the fourth left-right-left, none of which is a mirror image of D-fructose. Answer (C).
authoredSolutions.32: Take the four drawn pairs in turn. A is pentan-3-one (ethyl-CO-ethyl) with pentan-2-one (methyl-CO-propyl): same molecular formula \(C_{5}H_{10}O\), same functional group, different alkyl groups flanking the carbonyl, so they are metamers. B is butanenitrile \(C_{3}H_{7}-C\equiv N\) with propyl isocyanide \(C_{3}H_{7}-N\equiv C\): same formula \(C_{4}H_{7}N\) but different functional groups, so functional isomers. C is butan-1-ol with butan-2-ol: same formula \(C_{4}H_{10}O\) and same OH group, only its position differs, so position isomers. D pairs a primary amine with a secondary amine, which belong to different classes and so are not members of one homologous series. A, B and C are correct, which is option (d), the fourth option. Note that A, B and C are each individually correct, so the fourth option is forced whatever one decides about D.
authoredSolutions.33: For a fixed mass \(m\), number of atoms \(= (m/M)N_{A}\), so the element with the SMALLEST molar mass gives the largest number of atoms. authoredSolutions.34: A is false: electron gain is not always exothermic. Noble gases, and also Be, Mg and N with their stable filled or half-filled configurations, have positive (endothermic) electron gain enthalpies. B is true: removing an electron always requires energy against the nuclear attraction, so ionisation enthalpy is always positive, i.e. endothermic. C is true: \(IE_{1}\) of Be is about 899 kJ mol\(^{-1}\) and of B about 801 kJ mol\(^{-1}\), the drop arising because boron loses a less penetrating 2p electron while beryllium has a filled \(2s^{2}\) shell. D is false: electronegativity is not a fixed atomic constant, it depends on the bonded environment, so carbon does not carry an identical value in \(CH_{4}\) and \(CCl_{4}\). E is false: electropositive character increases down group 1, so Li is the LEAST electropositive alkali metal. Only B and C, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.35: The question turns entirely on the intensive versus extensive distinction. Molar heat capacity, density and concentration are all intensive: they are ratios of two extensive quantities and are therefore independent of how much material the system contains. Gibbs free energy is extensive, scaling directly with the amount of substance present. So on going from solution 1 to solution 2, whatever change of amount is depicted, the only listed property that can change is the Gibbs free energy. Answer (D).
authoredSolutions.36: The iodoform test needs either a methyl ketone fragment \(CH_{3}-CO-\) or a \(CH_{3}-CH(OH)-\) group that \(I_{2}/OH^{-}\) can first oxidise to a methyl ketone. Going through the list: ethanol has \(CH_{3}CH(OH)H\), gives; isopropyl alcohol has \(CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}\), gives; bromoacetone \(CH_{3}COCH_{2}Br\) has an intact methyl ketone, gives; butan-2-ol has \(CH_{3}CH(OH)-\), gives; butan-2-one \(CH_{3}COC_{2}H_{5}\), gives; pentan-2-one \(CH_{3}COC_{3}H_{7}\), gives. The failures are butanal (aldehyde, no methyl ketone), pentan-3-one (ethyl on both sides of C=O), pentanal, and pentan-3-ol (the carbinol carbon carries two ethyl groups, not a methyl). That is 4 molecules, option (B).
authoredSolutions.37: The middle species drawn in the scheme is benzenediazonium chloride, and the reagent that produced it is \(NaNO_{2}/HCl\) at 273-278 K, which is diazotisation of a primary aromatic amine. Therefore [A] is aniline, \(C_{6}H_{5}NH_{2}\); nitrobenzene cannot be diazotised. Treating the diazonium salt with KI replaces \(N_{2}^{+}\) by iodine without any copper catalyst, so [B] is iodobenzene, \(C_{6}H_{5}I\). Finally 2Na in dry ether is the Fittig coupling of two aryl halides, giving biphenyl as [C]. The option showing aniline, iodobenzene and biphenyl is the third one.
authoredSolutions.38: Reaction (A) as drawn claims benzenediazonium chloride plus ethanol gives phenetole, \(C_{6}H_{5}OC_{2}H_{5}\). That is wrong: ethanol acts as a REDUCING agent towards arenediazonium salts, delivering a hydride and being itself oxidised to ethanal, so the product is benzene together with \(N_{2}\), \(CH_{3}CHO\) and HCl. The other three are all standard and correct: \(H_{3}PO_{2}/H_{2}O\) likewise reduces the diazonium group to H giving benzene (B); KI substitutes iodine directly to give iodobenzene (C); and CuCN/KCN is the Sandmeyer reaction giving benzonitrile (D). authoredSolutions.39: The wavelength absorbed is set by the crystal field splitting through \(\Delta_{o} = hc/\lambda\), so the strongest field absorbs the SHORTEST wavelength. From the spectrochemical series the ligand field strength runs \(CN^{-} > NH_{3} > H_{2}O > Cl^{-}\). Hence \(\Delta_{o}\) decreases in the order \([Co(CN)_{6}]^{3-}\) (C) \(> [Co(NH_{3})_{6}]^{3+}\) (B) \(> [Co(NH_{3})_{5}(H_{2}O)]^{3+}\) (A, one \(NH_{3}\) replaced by the weaker \(H_{2}O\)) \(> [CoCl(NH_{3})_{5}]^{2+}\) (D, weakest since \(Cl^{-}\) is the poorest of the four). Inverting for wavelength gives \(D > A > B > C\), option (A).
authoredSolutions.40: Xenon is chemically inert here, so \(K_{p}\) is untouched. But the addition is at constant temperature AND constant total pressure, so the container must expand to accommodate the xenon; the partial pressures of all reacting gases fall. Writing \(K_{p} = \frac{p_{PCl_{3}}p_{Cl_{2}}}{p_{PCl_{5}}}\), an equal fractional reduction of every partial pressure divides the numerator by a factor squared and the denominator by that factor only, so the reaction quotient falls below \(K_{p}\) and the system responds by shifting forward, towards the side with more gas molecules \((\Delta n_{g} = +1)\). More \(PCl_{5}\) dissociates, so \(PCl_{3}\) and \(Cl_{2}\) both increase while \(PCl_{5}\) decreases. Answer (D). Note that if the inert gas were added at constant VOLUME instead, nothing would move.
authoredSolutions.41: Both ethylene glycol and glucose are non-volatile non-electrolytes, so neither dissociates and the van't Hoff factor is 1 for each; boiling point elevation depends only on the TOTAL number of solute particles. Total solute \(= 2 + 2 = 4\) mol in 0.500 kg of water, giving molality \(m = 4/0.5 = 8\) mol kg\(^{-1}\). Then \(\Delta T_{b} = K_{b}m = 0.52 \times 8 = 4.16\) K, and \(T_{b} = 373.15 + 4.16 = 377.31\) K, which is 377.3 K. Answer (B).
authoredSolutions.42: Work backwards from 3-methyl-6-oxoheptanal, \(OHC-CH_{2}-CH(CH_{3})-CH_{2}-CH_{2}-CO-CH_{3}\). Both carbonyls sit in ONE molecule, so the precursor must be a cyclic alkene whose ring was cut open by ozonolysis; joining C1 to C6 closes a six-membered ring with the C7 methyl left as a substituent on the ketone carbon. The ring is therefore cyclohexene bearing a methyl on one alkene carbon and a second methyl three carbons away, which is 1,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene. Checking forwards: cleaving \(C1=C2\) of that alkene makes the methyl-substituted carbon a methyl ketone and the other alkene carbon an aldehyde, and the remaining methyl ends up on the third carbon from the CHO end, giving exactly 3-methyl-6-oxoheptanal. Of the four drawings, only the second is 1,4-dimethylcyclohexene; the others are the 1,5-, 1,3- and 1,6-isomers. Answer (B).
authoredSolutions.43: \(PF_{5}\): phosphorus has 5 bond pairs and no lone pair, a trigonal bipyramid, so \(sp^{3}d\), which is II. \(SF_{6}\): 6 bond pairs, octahedral, so \(sp^{3}d^{2}\), which is III. \(Ni(CO)_{4}\): CO is a strong field ligand, \(Ni(0)\) is \(3d^{10}4s^{0}\) with no unpaired electrons and no vacant inner d orbital available, so the tetrahedral geometry arises from \(sp^{3}\), which is IV. \([PtCl_{4}]^{2-}\): \(Pt(II)\) is \(5d^{8}\); with the heavy 5d metal the electrons pair up leaving one d orbital vacant, giving square planar \(dsp^{2}\), which is I. So A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I, option (A).
authoredSolutions.44: Rank the four by the stability of the anion left after losing the proton. Compound B, benzenesulfonic acid, is a very strong acid \((pK_{a}\) about \(-2.8)\) since the charge is spread over three oxygens. Compound C, butanoic acid, has \(pK_{a}\) about 4.8, the carboxylate being resonance stabilised over two oxygens. Compound A, 3-ethoxyphenol, is a phenol with \(pK_{a}\) near 10, delocalisation into the ring being much less effective than into a carboxylate. Compound D, ethyl propiolate \(EtO_{2}C-C\equiv CH\), loses a terminal alkyne proton; even with the ester group helping, the sp carbanion is far less stabilised and the \(pK_{a}\) stays around 20 or higher, i.e. very much the weakest acid. So the least acidic compound is D, and the option carrying D is the first one, (A).
authoredSolutions.45: Limiting molar conductivities of cations in water at 298 K (in S cm\(^{2}\) mol\(^{-1}\)) are \(H^{+}\) 349.6, \(Ca^{2+}\) 119.0, \(Mg^{2+}\) 106.0, \(K^{+}\) 73.5 and \(Na^{+}\) 50.1. The proton is far ahead of everything else because it moves by the Grotthuss hopping mechanism through the hydrogen-bonded network rather than by bodily migration. The divalent ions beat the monovalent ones because each carries twice the charge, and within each charge type the smaller hydrated radius wins, so \(Ca^{2+} > Mg^{2+}\) (the smaller bare \(Mg^{2+}\) is more heavily hydrated and therefore effectively bigger and slower) and \(K^{+} > Na^{+}\) for the same reason. Order: \(H^{+} > Ca^{2+} > Mg^{2+} > K^{+} > Na^{+}\), option (B).
authoredSolutions.46: The figure shows compound X as piperazine, a six-membered ring of four \(CH_{2}\) groups and two NH groups placed para to each other, so \(X = C_{4}H_{10}N_{2}\). Its molar mass is \(4(12) + 10(1) + 2(14) = 86\) g mol\(^{-1}\). Moles of X \(= 0.42/86 = 4.884 \times 10^{-3}\). In Dumas' method every nitrogen ends up in \(N_{2}\), and each molecule holds 2 N atoms, so moles of \(N_{2}\) equal moles of X, \(4.884 \times 10^{-3}\). At STP the molar volume is 22.7 L mol\(^{-1}\), giving \(V = 4.884 \times 10^{-3} \times 22700 = 110.9\) mL, i.e. 111 mL to the nearest integer.
authoredSolutions.47: In Liebig combustion every carbon atom of the compound is captured as \(CO_{2}\), so the mass of carbon is \((12/44)\) of the mass of \(CO_{2}\). Percentage of carbon \(= \frac{12}{44} \times \frac{\text{mass of } CO_{2}}{\text{mass of compound}} \times 100 = \frac{12}{44} \times \frac{1.46}{0.5} \times 100 = 0.2727 \times 2.92 \times 100 = 79.6\%\), which is 80 to the nearest integer. The water figure is not needed for this part; it would give the hydrogen percentage.
authoredSolutions.48: Oxalic acid in the presence of KOH supplies the oxalate dianion, a symmetrical bidentate O,O-donor. authoredSolutions.101: Read the three straight segments of the plot. From 0 to 2.0 mL the conductance FALLS (A to B): highly mobile \(H^{+}\) from the fully ionised HCl is being replaced by the much slower \(Na^{+}\), so this leg neutralises the strong acid. From 2.0 to 5.0 mL the conductance rises only gently (B to C): here the feebly ionised \(CH_{3}COOH\) is converted to fully ionised sodium acetate, a small net gain in ions. Beyond 5.0 mL the sharp rise (C to D) is free excess NaOH. So HCl needs 2.0 mL and acetic acid \(5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0\) mL of 0.1 M NaOH. Moles HCl \(= 0.1 \times 2.0 = 0.2\) mmol in 40 mL, giving \(0.2/40 = 0.005\) M, so (B) is correct. Acetic acid works out at \(0.3/40 = 0.0075\) M, not 0.005 M, ruling out (A); the strong acid is neutralised first, ruling out (C); and it is point B, not C, that marks complete neutralisation of HCl, ruling out (D).

That is poured into a 100 mL flask that already contains 2 MOLES of HCl and made up to the mark, so the final concentration of HCl is \(2\text{ mol}/0.100\text{ L} = 20\) M. The solution in the flask is therefore 20 M HCl, option (B).

authoredSolutions.104: All four symbols are superheavy elements at the foot of period 7, so each family is identified by its group. authoredSolutions.105: The orbital angular momentum is \(\sqrt{l(l+1)}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}\) and depends only on the azimuthal quantum number \(l\), never on \(n\). For a 2s electron \(l = 0\), so the orbital angular momentum is exactly zero. For a 2p electron \(l = 1\), giving \(\sqrt{1(1+1)}\,\frac{h}{2\pi} = \sqrt{2}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}\). Taken in the order asked, 2s then 2p, the values are 0 and \(\sqrt{2}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}\), option (D). Option (C) is the trap: \(\sqrt{6}\,\frac{h}{2\pi}\) belongs to \(l = 2\), a d electron.
authoredSolutions.106: A primary standard must be obtainable pure, be stable in air, be non-hygroscopic so that a weighed mass is a known mass, and have a definite composition. Sodium dichromate, \(Na_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}\), is deliquescent, which is precisely why the POTASSIUM salt and not the sodium salt is used as the standard oxidant, so A fails. NaOH is strongly hygroscopic and also absorbs atmospheric \(CO_{2}\) to form carbonate, so its weighed mass is never its true mass and C fails. Hydrated ferrous sulphate is readily air-oxidised to iron(III) and also effloresces, so its titre drifts and D fails; the stable substitute is Mohr's salt.
